title: MCP 2026-07-28: The Stateless Specification
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol published its **2026-07-28 specification** — the largest revision since MCP launched in November 2024. The headline change: MCP moves from a stateful, connection-oriented protocol to a **stateless core**. Previously, an MCP client and server had to establish and maintain an open session; now each request carries everything a server needs to handle it on its own.

---

## Why Statelessness Matters

Under the old model, a long-lived session tied a client to one specific server process, which made horizontal scaling awkward — you needed sticky routing or shared session storage across server replicas. Under the stateless core, requests can be load-balanced across any available server instance with no shared storage required, which matters a lot for production MCP deployments behind multiple replicas.

---

## Key Additions

- **Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR)** — lets a single logical operation span multiple request/response exchanges without holding a session open.
- **Header-based routing** — routing information moves into request headers rather than depending on connection state.
- **Cacheable list results** — `tools/list`, `resources/list`, etc. can now be cached more aggressively since they no longer depend on session state.
- **Authorization hardening** — validation rules were tightened to match how OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect are actually deployed in practice, including mandatory validation of the `iss` (issuer) parameter to block a class of "mix-up" attack where a token issued for one authorization server is replayed against another.
- **Formal extensions framework** — a standard mechanism for shipping protocol features (like the new Tasks extension, below) outside the core spec, so they can iterate faster without destabilizing the base protocol.
- **Updated Tier 1 SDKs** — the TypeScript and Python SDKs were updated to match; both have now crossed 1 billion total downloads, with close to half a billion combined downloads per month across Tier 1 SDKs.

---

## Deprecations

Three capabilities move to deprecated status. They continue to work for **at least twelve months**, but new implementations shouldn't build on them:

| Deprecated | Replacement |
|---|---|
| Roots | Tool parameters |
| Sampling | Direct calls to an LLM provider API |
| Logging | OpenTelemetry |

**Tasks** move out of the experimental core entirely and into a formal `io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks` extension, with a poll-based `tasks/get` and a new `tasks/update` method for long-running operations.

**Change notifications** move from the old HTTP GET endpoint into a single `subscriptions/listen` stream that clients opt into per notification type, rather than receiving everything by default.

The legacy **HTTP+SSE transport** is also now officially deprecated, with the same year-long offramp as the other changes.

---

## What This Means for MCP Clients Like Claude Code

Existing MCP servers built against the older, stateful spec keep working during the twelve-month deprecation window — this isn't a hard break. But new server development should target the stateless core and the Tasks extension instead of Roots, Sampling, or Logging, since those paths are on a fixed retirement clock. Anthropic maintains a curated list of community MCP servers at `github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers`; server authors there are expected to migrate over the same window.
